narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 95.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission and wants students likely to succeed, this strong prediction of failure led directly to the rejection of your application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, both pushing the model heavily toward predicting failure. Being in the second decile after your first year and the bottom decile after your third year placed you far below the average performance of accepted students, who typically ranked around the sixth decile. These academic standing indicators were the clearest signals the model used.

Your LSAT score of 28 was the third most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure. It sits well below the average of 37 among students who were admitted.

Other details such as your undergraduate GPA of 2.7, middle family income, full-time study plans, gender, and Asian background played much smaller roles and were not major drivers of the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score significantly. These steps would most directly address the factors that weighed against your application. (218 words)
